transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-13
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~30 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramirez (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SRE), Priya Shah (Acadia Lead ML Eng), Ethan Brooks (Acadia Platform Eng), Lena Ortiz (CTO), Marco Diaz (Security), Jonah Reed (Data)

Auto-summary: quick review of TTFT numbers, streaming heuristics experiments, and an ask to pick kernels for the pilot. Security asked for KMS confirmation.

[00:00] Maya Chen: ok hi everybody thanks for joining, we'll keep this tight — agenda is TTFT numbers, streaming heuristics, kernel pick for short sequences, and action items.
[01:00] Priya Shah: hey thanks Maya, quick context, we ran your latest agent build on our dev cluster overnight, saw overall token throughput increase but first token latency jumped on the 32-64 token bucket, so that's our big itch.
[02:00] Diego Ramirez: yeah thanks Priya, we saw that too — looks like the continuous batching path flipped to a different kernel after the 32 token threshold, which impacts cold kv cache warms and increases T-T-F-T a bit.
[03:00] Ethan Brooks: just to call out our distribution — about 58% of requests are sub-50 tokens, 30% 50-200, rest tail. we'll drop the percentile csv in the sheet.
[04:00] Maya Chen: perfect — Priya, can you confirm that 58% number is p50 or p75? we need exact percentiles to pick bucket boundaries.
[05:00] Priya Shah: p50 is 42, p75 89, median's lower but the mode sits around 28 tokens; I'll upload the 1k sample soon.
[06:00] Diego Ramirez: quick notes — on the runtime side we have two candidate kernels: fast-init short-seq kernel (fisher-k) that is great for <48 tokens but degrades for long streaming; and slab-stream kernel that's better for continuous kv cache reuse. switching between them adds about 5-7ms overhead when we re-route mid-request.
[07:00] Maya Chen: so tradeoff is static pick for most requests vs hedging and paying switch overhead. What's the measured overhead in your bench? link?
[08:00] Diego Ramirez: I uploaded a trimmed bench sheet — https://redwood.share/bench/acadia-ttft-v2 (note: internal link, redacted for sec). you can see microbench rows 12-18 that show 6ms median switch cost with microburst enabled.
[09:00] Lena Ortiz: is that 6ms per request or per switch? under bursty traffic that could add up.
[10:00] Diego Ramirez: it's per switch event; if we hop kernels mid-stream during long responses, that overhead is incurred once per request. but if the pipeline picks the wrong kernel many times, you accumulate.
[11:00] Marco Diaz: from security, we want to confirm that switching kernels doesn't cause any additional KV cache leakage or expand the attack surface — also need confirmation on KMS and audit logs.
[12:00] Samir Patel: switching kernels doesn't transmit additional user data off-host; it's an internal exec path. for KMS we support customer-managed keys (HSM-backed) and can provide audit log examples, I'll share the network diagram.
[13:00] Jonah Reed: small note, we saw a few transcription artefacts in the logs where model id was 'lamda-600' instead of 'llama-6k' — not important but may confuse the filtering.
[14:00] Priya Shah: yep saw that also, the agent called it 'lamda' in some traces.
[15:00] Diego Ramirez: that's a transcription mismatch in the local tracer, we'll normalize in the next upload.
[16:00] Ethan Brooks: on streaming heuristics — we tried the early-response sampler at 5 token window, it shaved average first-response by ~12% but increased tail variance.
[17:00] Maya Chen: what's the tail increase? small? unacceptable?
[18:00] Ethan Brooks: p95 moved from 210ms to 280ms in that run, so noticeable.
[19:00] Diego Ramirez: that aligns with the idea — early-response sampling takes a conservative small chunk off the buffer and responds sooner but sometimes forces extra context prep for the stream. we have two knobs: sample size and backlog threshold.
[20:00] Priya Shah: we care more about p50/p60 in our UI for diagnostics, but customer-facing product needs p95 to be stable — leaning toward conservative sample size.
[21:00] Maya Chen: recommendation from SE side?
[22:00] Diego Ramirez: for your distribution (mode ~28 tokens), I recommend enabling the fast-init short-seq kernel by default and a small early-sample of 3 tokens at the very first pass; that gives good p50 benefit and keeps p95 within 10% of baseline. Also add a microburst hedging policy to route >200t to slab-stream.
[23:00] Lena Ortiz: ok but what about quantization — we tested int8 and saw a small TTFT regression. is that expected?
[24:00] Samir Patel: int8 helps throughput but can add a decode cost for first token because of quant dequant steps if we're not using quant-aware kernels. we recommend per-model quant profiles — some models get int8 safe kernels that keep TTFT flat.
[25:00] Maya Chen: we'll include a quant recommendation table in the notebook. Diego, can you log the quant vs TTFT rows in the sheet?
[26:00] Diego Ramirez: yes will add rows comparing fp16, int8 and q4_0 variants tonight.
[27:00] Marco Diaz: security request — please share SOC2 evidence for access logs, and a redacted runbook for incidents. I'll capture required fields and send to Maya.
[28:00] Maya Chen: noted, Marco. I'll follow up with the security pack link — https://redwood.share/sec/acadia-pkg.pdf — and we'll redact before posting.
[29:00] Priya Shah: one practical ask — can we run a microburst test that simulates 250 concurrent short (10-30 token) requests over 60s window? we want to see eviction/hedge behavior.
[30:00] Diego Ramirez: yes we'll run that; I'll add logs to the bench.

Recap and next steps:
- Diego to run microburst test and attach logs to bench (due 2026-07-20).
- Priya to upload 1k request samples with seq len distribution (due 2026-07-16).
- Samir to validate VPC egress & share diagram (due 2026-07-22).
- Maya to circulate trimmed benchmark spreadsheet with TTFT highlights (due 2026-07-14).
- Marco to provide required SOC2 fields and redaction guidance (due 2026-07-19).

End of transcript.
